title: [Project] CSS Flag
summary: Capstone for the Intermediate CSS section: rebuild the flag of Laos from a fixed, class-light HTML file using only CSS. It exercises combinators, specificity, the cascade and absolute/relative positioning. The walkthrough also shows Chrome's 'copy selector' as a shortcut for targeting unlabeled elements.

concepts.heading: Why the project exists
points: The intro showcases CSS art (a painted portrait and a Simpsons set built from divs with border-radius, width, height and colours) to show how far plain CSS goes. The flag is deliberately far smaller than those.
Constraint: index.html must not be edited. There are almost no classes or IDs, so the selectors have to come from structure (child and descendant combinators) and from positioning knowledge.
Skills being tested: combining selectors, specificity and cascade, and position relative/absolute. Exact placement is not graded; roughly matching the goal image is enough.

concepts.heading: Reading the HTML structure
points: Outer div.flag is the red rectangle. Its children are a p (title text), then a div (blue rectangle).
Inside the blue div sits another div (the white circle), which contains a p with the second line of text.
So: .flag > div selects the blue box, and .flag > div > div (or .flag div div) selects the circle. Both are structural selectors, not class-based.
(Extra) Hints in the HTML comments give the flag size and circle size; the flag colours were read from the real flag image.

concepts.heading: Getting exact colours
points: Inspect the flag image in Chrome DevTools, open the three-dot menu, More tools, CSS overview, then Capture overview. It lists the hex colours found (red #ce1126, blue #002868).
This re-uses the colour-picking technique from the earlier inspection lesson.

concepts.heading: Step-by-step build
points: Red rectangle: .flag gets width 900px, height 600px and the red background-color.
Blue rectangle: .flag > div gets width 100% (equivalent to 900px, taken from the parent), height 300px (half the red box) and the blue background.
Circle: .flag > div > div gets width 200px, height 200px, white background, then border-radius 50% turns the square into a circle.

Layout of blue box: it should sit a quarter of the flag height (150px) down. Make .flag position: relative (it does not move; it becomes the reference) and the blue div position: absolute with top: 150px. This relative-parent / absolute-child pairing is the standard pattern.

Centre the circle in the blue box: blue is 900x300 and circle is 200x200, so top = (300-200)/2 = 50px and left = (900-200)/2 = 350px. For the offsets to refer to the blue box, the blue box itself must be a positioned element, which absolute positioning provides.

Why a naive centring looked off: the default margins on the p elements stayed in normal flow and pushed content down. Deleting them in DevTools fixed it, so the code sets p { margin: 0 } (padding 0 too in the solution).
Text: font-size 5rem on all p, text-align: center to centre both lines. The Pesticide extension / DevTools was used to see the paragraph box that caused the offset.

concepts.heading: Text colours and the 'copy selector' trick
points: Easiest approach: set all p to white, then override only the circle's p to black. The default colour is already black, so alternatively only the top p could be made white.
Targeting the circle's p without classes: in the Elements panel, right-click the element, Copy, Copy selector. This yields a long chain like body > div > div > div > p.
Do not paste blindly. Understand it and simplify: drop the body, swap in .flag, and replace > with spaces (descendant combinator), giving something like .flag div div p { color: black }.
This selector is more specific than the plain p rule, so it wins regardless of order (cascade and specificity).

task.name: Laos flag in pure CSS
task.starting_point: index.html with a div.flag containing a p, a div, and inside that div another div holding a p. HTML is fixed and has almost no classes; a goal.png and solution.html are provided.
task.goal: Using only CSS in the style block, recreate the flag: red field, blue band across the middle half, white circle centred in the band, a white heading line on top and black text inside the circle.
steps: Size the .flag div 900x600 and colour it red (#ce1126).
Select the blue child div with .flag > div, size it to 100% x 300px and colour it #002868.
Select the circle div (grandchild), size 200x200, white, border-radius 50%.
Make .flag position: relative; make the blue div absolute with top 150px; make the circle absolute with top 50px and left 350px.
Remove default paragraph margins and set font-size 5rem and text-align center.
Make the top text white and the circle's text black using a descendant selector.
task.expected_result: A 900x600 flag: red top and bottom quarters, a blue band in the middle, a white circle in its centre with black text, white title text at the top.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 07 - Intermediate CSS/07.04 - CSS Flag Project/solution.html

pitfalls: Forgetting position: relative on the parent, so absolute offsets are measured from the page instead of from the flag.
Leaving default p margins, which shift the content and make the circle look off-centre.
Pasting a long copied selector without understanding it; simplify it so it stays readable.
(Extra) The repo's index.html is a student's own attempt (relative blue box at top: 60px, author footer), not the starter; use solution.html as the reference and ignore the 'Made with' footer.

playground.coverage: Covers the relative-parent / absolute-child centring with a simple flag (Japan-style circle) and gives the centring maths and the translate(-50%,-50%) alternative.
gaps_and_ideas: The playground has classes on every element; the real project forbids editing HTML. Add a variant task using only structural selectors (.flag > div, .flag > div > div).
Add the DevTools 'Copy selector then simplify' exercise.
Include the paragraph-margin gotcha and a toggle in an explore demo that shows margins pushing content.
Add a three-layer version (red, blue band, circle) matching the Laos flag, with hex colours and a CSS overview tip.
